intro: Read the deck for the law and these notes for the thinking. Each note under a slide says what to remember, how to use it and where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself with the recall questions, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: Why child rights
sections.big_idea: Children hold claims of their own, so a programme must ask **who owes what** as well as who needs help.
in_plain_words: The welfare view treats children as objects of care. The rights view treats them as holders of claims against the state. A child who goes unhelped under welfare has bad luck. Under rights that child has been wronged, and someone has a duty to put it right.

Four questions turn the idea into practice: who is left out, whose interest decides, is the child safe, and was the child heard. Add the duty bearers, from the state to parents, and the three numbers on scale, and you can read any scheme. **Watch for rights language used to control children.**

right.title: The rights view
items: The state can be asked to account
Takes the child's views into account

diagram.caption: the same child, two ways of seeing the duty

key_terms.meaning: Entitlements of every person below eighteen, set out in the CRC and national law.
The person or body that owes a right: state, statutory body, institution, parent.
Survival and development, protection, participation, and cross-cutting duties.
A primary consideration in all actions concerning children (Article 3).
Confining or rescuing a child in ways the child would not accept.

worked_example.title: Which frame is this scheme using?
worked_example.setup: A donor log-frame for a school meal programme reports only the number of beneficiaries each month.
steps: Ask whether children were asked anything. The log-frame records no consultation.
Ask who owes the child what. The log-frame names no duty bearer and no complaint route.
Count what is measured: beneficiaries only, which is the welfare habit the slide describes.
Add the four rights questions: who is left out, whose interest decides, is the child safe, was the child heard.
worked_example.answer: The log-frame sits in the welfare frame. Adding the four questions and a named duty bearer moves it toward a rights frame.

mistakes: Reading one frame into every South Asian policy. Most policy mixes the welfare and rights views, so check each document.
Treating the four rights questions as a legal exercise. The slide says none of them needs a lawyer.
Reading the crime count as a trend in abuse. It counts First Information Reports, so reporting changes it too.
Using protective language to justify confinement or rescue without consent.

recall.q: What are the four questions a rights frame adds to a needs assessment?
recall.a: Who is left out, whose interest decides, is the child safe, and was the child heard.

recall.q: Name the four families of rights.
recall.a: Survival and development, protection, participation, and cross-cutting duties.

recall.q: Why can a rise in registered crimes against children mislead?
recall.a: It can mean more abuse, more reporting, or both, because the count is of First Information Reports.

recall.q: What is the test for any intervention?
recall.a: Would the child, once old enough to judge, agree that it was done for them?

recall.q: Which section of POCSO makes reporting a duty for any person?
recall.a: Section 19(1).

sections.title: The Convention and its four principles
sections.big_idea: The CRC is the common text every government, donor and NGO can be held to, built on **four principles** that apply to every right.
in_plain_words: The Convention was adopted on 20 November 1989, entered into force on 2 September 1990 and now has 196 States parties. Every South Asian state is a party. India acceded on 11 December 1992 without signing, with a declaration on Article 32, child labour.

Four articles carry the weight: Article 2 on non-discrimination, Article 3(1) on best interests, Article 6 on life, survival and development, and Article 12 on the child's views. Read them as a set. **Use the grid of principles against any situation** and treat a blank cell as an unanswered question.

events.what: Adopted by the UN General Assembly

diagram.caption: how the Convention reached South Asia

key_terms.meaning: Joining a treaty without signing first; same legal effect as ratification.
Article 2: rights for each child within the state's jurisdiction.
Article 3(1): a primary consideration in all actions concerning children.
Article 12: views weighed by age and maturity.
A state's stated understanding on an article, such as India on Article 32.

worked_example.title: Count the parts of the Convention
worked_example.setup: The Convention has 54 articles. Part I runs from Article 1 to 41 and Part II from Article 42 to 45.
steps: Part I holds 41 articles, because it runs from 1 to 41.
Part II holds 45 − 41 = 4 articles.
Together, Parts I and II hold 41 + 4 = 45 articles.
Part III is what remains: 54 − 45 = 9 articles.
worked_example.answer: Part III has 9 articles, covering signature and entry into force.

mistakes: Calling India a signatory. India acceded without signing, which has the same effect as ratification.
Reading Article 3 as making best interests the only consideration. It is "a primary consideration", except in adoption where it is paramount.
Hearing a child and ignoring the answer. Article 12 needs both expression and due weight.
Quoting a state's reservations from memory. Check the current UN Treaty Collection text.

recall.q: When did the Convention enter into force?
recall.a: 2 September 1990.

recall.q: Which article is the non-discrimination principle?
recall.a: Article 2.

recall.q: What does Article 12 require beyond letting a child speak?
recall.a: The child's views must be given due weight according to age and maturity.

recall.q: What did India declare on Article 32?
recall.a: That it would progressively implement the article, particularly paragraph 2(a), and that setting minimum ages immediately was not practical.

recall.q: Which General comment treats best interests as a right, a principle and a rule of procedure?
recall.a: General comment No. 14 (2013).

sections.title: Protocols, the Committee and reporting
sections.big_idea: Three optional protocols and an 18-member Committee give the Convention teeth, but **India's children have no individual complaint route** to Geneva.
in_plain_words: The first protocol covers children in armed conflict, the second sale of children and sexual exploitation, and the third a complaints procedure. Every South Asian state accepted the first two, and only the Maldives accepted the third. States declared different recruitment ages, because voluntary recruitment below eighteen is allowed with safeguards.

The Committee reviews state reports in a cycle: report, alternative reports, list of issues, dialogue, concluding observations and follow-up. **Practitioners enter at the alternative report.** India's last full review was in 2014, and its general comments give you language to cite.

diagram.caption: the periodic review loop; practitioners enter at step two

key_terms.meaning: Optional protocol on children in armed conflict.
Optional protocol on sale, prostitution and pornography.
Protocol letting children complain to the Committee.
The Committee's published recommendations after a review.
The Committee's authoritative reading of an article or theme.
Civil society's own evidence to the Committee.

worked_example.title: How long since India's last review?
worked_example.setup: India's concluding observations were adopted on 13 June 2014. The reporting rhythm after the first report is five years, and the slide is dated October 2026.
steps: Years since the review: 2026 − 2014 = 12.
Reports are expected every 5 years, so one cycle is 5 years.
Years beyond one cycle: 12 − 5 = 7.
The slide's own wording is that more than twelve years have passed.
worked_example.answer: About 12 years since the last review, 7 years past one five-year cycle.

mistakes: Telling an Indian family the UN Committee can hear their complaint. India is not a party to the complaints protocol.
Treating a general comment as a treaty. It is the Committee's reading and carries weight through use.
Waiting for the Committee to order change. Its output is observations and recommendations, without binding judgments.
Submitting separate NGO reports. One coalition report carries more weight than ten.

recall.q: How many experts sit on the Committee?
recall.a: Eighteen.

recall.q: Which South Asian state accepted the complaints protocol?
recall.a: The Maldives, ratifying on 27 September 2019.

recall.q: When is a state's first report due and how often afterwards?
recall.a: Two years after the Convention enters into force for it, then every five years.

recall.q: What is the useful procedural idea in General comment No. 14?
recall.a: The decision-making process must include an evaluation of the impact of the decision on the child.

recall.q: Which general comment deals with public budgeting?

sections.title: India's constitutional framework
sections.big_idea: The Constitution gives children **enforceable rights** in Part III and **guiding principles** in Part IV, and the difference decides what you can demand in court.
in_plain_words: Articles 15(3), 21A and 24 sit in Part III and can be enforced through the High Courts and the Supreme Court. Articles 39(e), 39(f) and 45 are directive principles that no court enforces directly, yet courts read them with Article 21. Article 51A(k) adds a duty for parents.

Education became a fundamental right only in 2002, and the RTE Act came into effect on 1 April 2010. Courts then built more rights from Article 21, in the Sivakasi order and in cases on marriage. **Check which definition of child applies**, because Indian law uses many ages.

key_terms.meaning: Free and compulsory education for children six to fourteen.
A guiding principle in Part IV that no court enforces directly.
Enforceable by a court, as Part III rights are.
A High Court's writ power to enforce rights.
The 2002 Act that inserted Article 21A.

worked_example.title: Which article gives the claim?
worked_example.setup: Three children: a four-year-old, an eight-year-old and a fifteen-year-old.
steps: The four-year-old falls under Article 45, a directive principle, so the claim is weaker.
The eight-year-old is within six to fourteen, so Article 21A and the RTE Act apply.
The fifteen-year-old is outside the RTE age band, so Article 21A does not apply.
Article 24 bars hazardous employment only below fourteen, so it does not cover the fifteen-year-old either.
worked_example.answer: Article 45, Article 21A and the RTE Act, and none of the three for the fifteen-year-old.

mistakes: Calling early childhood care a fundamental right. Article 45 is a directive principle.
Quoting the 1950 Article 45 as current. The 2002 amendment rewrote it for children under six.
Assuming one age of childhood. The slide table shows nine different tests.
Reading Article 21A as a free-standing right. It operates "in such manner as the State may, by law, determine".

recall.q: Which articles are fundamental rights for children?
recall.a: Articles 15(3), 21A and 24.

recall.q: When did Article 21A and the RTE Act come into effect?
recall.a: 1 April 2010.

recall.q: What did the Sivakasi order require of employers?
recall.a: Rs 20,000 per child paid into a Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund.

recall.q: What did Independent Thought (2017) hold?
recall.a: Sexual intercourse with a girl below eighteen is rape regardless of whether she is married.

recall.q: What age is a child for POCSO?
recall.a: Under 18.

sections.title: Juvenile justice: the JJ Act 2015
sections.big_idea: One Act has **two doors**: a Board for children in conflict with law and a Committee for children in need of care, both guided by sixteen principles.
in_plain_words: A child in conflict with law goes before a Juvenile Justice Board, where bail is the rule and sentences of death or life without release are barred. A child in need of care goes before a Child Welfare Committee, which chooses between restoration, sponsorship, family-based care, adoption and an institution as a last resort.

The 2015 Act allows a preliminary assessment for sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds in heinous cases, and the 2021 amendment shifted adoption orders to the District Magistrate. **The Act also punishes adults**, including media that identify a child under section 74.

diagram.caption: the route for a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old

key_terms.meaning: A child alleged or found to have committed an offence while under eighteen.
A child in one of twelve situations listed in s. 2(14).
The body deciding cases of children in conflict with law.
The body deciding for children in need of care and protection.
One with a minimum punishment of seven years or more.
A working rule against labels such as "juvenile delinquent".

worked_example.title: Which body and which route?
worked_example.setup: A young man is arrested at nineteen for an act he committed at seventeen. It is alleged to be a heinous offence.
steps: The Act fixes age at the date of the offence, so he is treated as a child.
He is a child in conflict with law, so the Juvenile Justice Board hears the case.
He was seventeen at the time and the offence is heinous, so the Board conducts a preliminary assessment (s. 15(1)).
If trial as an adult is needed, the case moves to the Children's Court, but no death sentence or life without release can follow.
worked_example.answer: Juvenile Justice Board first, possibly the Children's Court, with the s. 21 limits in force throughout.

mistakes: Treating a working child picked up in a raid as an offender. That child is a child in need of care.
Keeping a child in a home "pending inquiry" for months. Delay is a decision, and it is usually the institution's.
Using an informal placement with a relative or hostel instead of a Committee order.
Publishing a case study that lets a reader identify a child in the system. Section 74 applies to NGOs too.

recall.q: Who decides for a child in need of care?
recall.a: The Child Welfare Committee, one or more in every district (s. 27).

recall.q: What is the rule on bail for a child?
recall.a: Release on bail or supervision is the rule, with three stated exceptions (s. 12(1)).

recall.q: What does section 21 bar?
recall.a: Sentences of death or life imprisonment without the possibility of release.

recall.q: What changed about adoption orders in 2021?
recall.a: The power moved from civil courts to the District Magistrate.

recall.q: Which section punishes media identification of a child?
recall.a: Section 74.

sections.title: Sexual offences: the POCSO Act 2012
sections.big_idea: POCSO protects every person under eighteen, requires **everyone to report**, and designs the trial around the child.
in_plain_words: The Act came into force on 14 November 2012 and defines offences without regard to the sex of victim or offender. It grades offences from harassment to penetrative assault and adds aggravated forms. The 2019 amendment raised minimums and added death as a possible sentence for aggravated penetrative assault.

Section 19 makes reporting a duty of any person, and section 21 punishes failure. The trial is child-friendly, with targets of thirty days for evidence and one year for trial. **Reporting overrides confidentiality**, which is why adolescents must be told in advance what a worker will have to do.

diagram.caption: support runs alongside the legal process

key_terms.meaning: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012.
A graded offence made worse by who commits it or the circumstances.
The duty on any person to report an offence to police.
A Court of Session designated in each district for POCSO trials.
Child sexual exploitation and abuse material, the preferred term.
Special Juvenile Police Unit.

worked_example.title: What the 2019 amendment changed
worked_example.setup: Minimum sentences before and after the 2019 amendment, from the slide.
steps: Penetrative sexual assault: the minimum rose from 7 to 10 years, a rise of 10 − 7 = 3 years.
For a child below sixteen the minimum became 20 years, which is 20 − 7 = 13 years above the old minimum.
Aggravated penetrative sexual assault: the minimum rose from 10 to 20 years, a rise of 20 − 10 = 10 years.
Death was also added as a possible sentence for the aggravated form.
worked_example.answer: Minimums rose by 3, 13 and 10 years in those three cases, and death became a possible sentence.

mistakes: Treating a counselling disclosure as confidential. POCSO section 19 binds counsellors, doctors and researchers.
Treating every adolescent relationship as abuse. Any act with a person under eighteen is an offence in law, and that can criminalise young people.
Forwarding suspected material to report it. Note the URL and use the police or the cybercrime portal.
Letting the statutory targets run unwatched. Thirty days and one year slip without follow-up.

recall.q: Who must report under section 19?
recall.a: Any person, including the child, who knows or fears an offence.

recall.q: What is the penalty for an institution head who fails to report a subordinate's offence?
recall.a: Up to one year and a fine (s. 21(2)).

recall.q: How soon must police inform the Committee and Special Court?
recall.a: Within twenty-four hours of a report.

recall.q: What did the Law Commission's 283rd Report recommend on age of consent?
recall.a: Keep it at eighteen, with guided judicial discretion in sentencing for sixteen- to eighteen-year-olds in some cases.

recall.q: What term should replace "child pornography"?
recall.a: Child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM).

sections.title: Education and child labour
sections.big_idea: Education law and labour law cover the same children, and the **gap at fourteen** is where they slip out of both.
in_plain_words: The RTE Act gives children aged six to fourteen a right to free and compulsory schooling in a neighbourhood school. Section 12(1)(c) reserves at least a quarter of Class I seats in unaided private schools, and section 17 bans physical punishment. The 2019 amendment changed section 16 so that states may allow holding back.

The 2016 labour amendment bans work below fourteen, with two exceptions, and bars hazardous work below eighteen. Rescue is only the start: **follow the child for a year** to see whether school replaced work. At fourteen the RTE guarantee ends as non-hazardous work becomes lawful.

key_terms.meaning: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009.
At least 25% of Class I seats for weaker and disadvantaged children.
Work by family members with the engagement of other persons.
A person aged 14 to 18 under the labour law.
District fund credited with employers' fines (s. 14B).

worked_example.title: A quarter of the seats
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a private unaided school has 80 seats in Class I and a School Management Committee of 12 members.
steps: Reserved seats under section 12(1)(c): at least 80 × 25 ÷ 100 = 20.
The Committee must have at least three-fourths parents or guardians.
Parent members: 12 × 3 ÷ 4 = 9.
Seats left for open admission at most: 80 − 20 = 60.
worked_example.answer: At least 20 reserved seats, and at least 9 of the 12 Committee members are parents or guardians.

mistakes: Reading the no-detention rule as it was in 2009. Section 16 was substituted in 2019 and states now differ.
Treating beating as acceptable discipline. Section 17 is absolute, and the JJ Act adds criminal routes.
Counting rescues as the outcome. The outcome is a child in school and not working a year later.
Forgetting children aged 14 to 18. They have no statutory right to free education under the RTE Act.

recall.q: What is the RTE age band?
recall.a: Six to fourteen years.

recall.q: What exceptions does the 2016 labour amendment allow for children under fourteen?
recall.a: Helping a family enterprise outside school hours or vacations, and working as an artist in audio-visual entertainment or sports.

recall.q: What is the penalty range under section 14?
recall.a: Six months to two years, or Rs 20,000 to Rs 50,000, or both.

recall.q: How many children aged 5 to 14 worked in India per Census 2011?
recall.a: 10.1 million, 3.9% of the age group.

recall.q: What is the weak point between education and labour law?
recall.a: At fourteen the RTE guarantee ends in the same year non-hazardous work becomes lawful.

sections.title: Child marriage
sections.big_idea: The law sets 18 for women and 21 for men and offers **tools before the wedding**, but prevention matters more than prosecution.
in_plain_words: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 makes a marriage voidable at the option of the party who was a child, and punishes adult men who marry children and those who perform or permit the marriage. The ages have stood since 1978, and a 2021 Bill to raise women's age to 21 lapsed in June 2024.

Marriage before eighteen is falling across South Asia, but the gradient inside India is steep by schooling, residence and state. Anyone can ask a magistrate for an injunction. **The 2024 Supreme Court judgment puts prevention first**, and a prosecution can harm the girl it is meant to protect.

diagram.caption: the preventive tools in the 2006 Act and JJ Act

key_terms.meaning: Valid until the party who was a child chooses to annul it.
A court order stopping a marriage before it happens.
Child Marriage Prohibition Officer.
An engagement made early, which the 2024 judgment flagged as an evasion route.
A fifth of the population, ordered by wealth.

worked_example.title: Reading the NFHS-5 gradient
worked_example.setup: Percentage of women 20 to 24 married by 18, NFHS-5: no schooling 45.9, secondary schooling 26.9, rural 25.8, urban 14.2, West Bengal 41.5, Kerala 6.3.
steps: Schooling gap: 45.9 − 26.9 = 19.0 percentage points.
Residence gap: 25.8 − 14.2 = 11.6 percentage points.
State gap: 41.5 − 6.3 = 35.2 percentage points.
India's headline fell from about 23 per cent to 20.1 per cent, a fall of 23 − 20.1 = 2.9 points.
worked_example.answer: The state gap is the largest at 35.2 points, followed by schooling at 19.0 and residence at 11.6.

mistakes: Reading the NFHS gradients as causes. They are associations that show where to look first.
Pressing charges without weighing the girl's interests. A father jailed can mean lost income and a blamed daughter.
Assuming the 2021 Bill raised the age. It lapsed, and the minimum ages remain 18 and 21.
Waiting for an offence. The injunction and the Child Welfare Committee are available before the wedding.

recall.q: What are the legal ages in the 2006 Act?
recall.a: 18 for females and 21 for males.

recall.q: Who can seek an injunction under section 13?
recall.a: Any person with knowledge, or an NGO with reasonable information, through a Judicial Magistrate.

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court say in October 2024 about enforcement?
recall.a: It must not be solely focused on increasing prosecutions without best efforts to prevent child marriage.

recall.q: What is the best evidence of age?
recall.a: A birth certificate.

recall.q: What penalty applies to disobeying an injunction?
recall.a: Up to two years, or a fine up to one lakh rupees, or both.

sections.title: Institutions and schemes
sections.big_idea: A rights claim needs a body to take it to: **commissions that inquire, schemes that deliver and a budget that pays**.
in_plain_words: The NCPCR and state commissions inquire into violations, monitor the RTE Act and POCSO, and hold civil court powers during an inquiry. They recommend and do not enforce, so follow each recommendation and escalate if nothing happens. A complaint costs nothing and needs no lawyer.

ICDS, since 1975, delivers six services to children under six, and Mission Vatsalya funds child protection bodies with Centre and State sharing costs. The Union Budget share for children has fallen by about half since 2012-13, with **protection a very small slice**. Keep a referral map with named district contacts.

key_terms.meaning: National Commission for Protection of Child Rights.
Integrated Child Development Services, since 1975.
Centrally sponsored child protection scheme that subsumed the earlier scheme.
Action a body takes on its own, without a complaint.
The Union Budget statement on spending for children.

worked_example.title: Splitting a scheme's cost
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a scheme component costs Rs 100 lakh. Use the Mission Vatsalya shares from the slide.
steps: Most states with a legislature share 60 : 40, so the Centre pays 100 × 60 ÷ 100 = 60 lakh.
The State pays 100 − 60 = 40 lakh.
For a North-Eastern state the shares are 90 : 10, so the Centre pays 100 × 90 ÷ 100 = 90 lakh.
A UT without a legislature is 100 : 0, so the Centre pays 100 lakh.
worked_example.answer: The Centre pays 60, 90 or 100 lakh depending on the area, and the State pays 40, 10 or nothing.

mistakes: Naming an old scheme in a proposal. Use Mission Vatsalya and the guidelines dated 5 July 2022.
Assuming a commission can order action. It recommends, so track what follows.
Assuming a right to an anganwadi place. Early childhood care is a directive principle.
Printing a referral map with no local names and numbers.

recall.q: What powers does the NCPCR have during an inquiry?
recall.a: Those of a civil court (s. 14).

recall.q: How many services does ICDS provide?
recall.a: Six.

recall.q: What was Mission Vatsalya's predecessor?
recall.a: The Child Protection Services scheme, running since 2009-10.

recall.q: What share of the children's budget goes to protection?
recall.a: 1.49 to 1.73 per cent.

recall.q: Who do you call for a child in danger now?
recall.a: Child Helpline 1098 or the police.

sections.title: Neighbours' frameworks
sections.big_idea: Each neighbour has written the Convention into its own law, and the **minimum age of criminal responsibility** varies from seven to twelve.
in_plain_words: Bangladesh's Children Act 2013 sets up Child Welfare Boards and Child Affairs Desks, though children's cases still go to a judicial court. Nepal's Act of 2018 covers rights, a National Child Rights Council and protection in the home, and names untouchability-based mistreatment.

Pakistan's 2018 Act bars the death sentence and corporal punishment for juvenile offenders and sets up diversion committees. Sri Lanka raised its age of responsibility to twelve in 2018, yet its 1939 Ordinance leaves older adolescents outside. **General comment 24 encourages at least 14.**

diagram.caption: the main child law in each country

key_terms.meaning: Bangladesh's Children Act 2013.
A desk at police stations headed by a Child Affairs Police Officer.
Handling a child's case outside formal court.
The age below which a child cannot be held criminally responsible.
Nepal's body chaired by the minister (s. 59).

worked_example.title: Distance from the 14-year benchmark
worked_example.setup: General comment 24 encourages states to set the minimum age of criminal responsibility at least at 14. Use India 7, Nepal 10 and Sri Lanka 12.
steps: India: 14 − 7 = 7 years below the benchmark.
Nepal: 14 − 10 = 4 years below.
Sri Lanka: 14 − 12 = 2 years below.
In India, anyone under eighteen is dealt with under the JJ Act, so the floor matters less than procedure.
worked_example.answer: India is 7 years below, Nepal 4 and Sri Lanka 2.

mistakes: Applying one country's definition of child to another. Sri Lanka's 1939 Ordinance says under 14.
Quoting reservations without checking. The slide says the UN Treaty Collection holds the current text.
Treating the minimum age of responsibility as the whole story. In India the JJ Act procedure matters more.
Assuming Pakistan's provincial laws match the federal Act. The slide does not cover them.

recall.q: How does Bangladesh define a child?
recall.a: Anyone up to eighteen (s. 4 of the Children Act 2013).

recall.q: What is Nepal's age below which no case lies?
recall.a: Under ten years (s. 36(1)).

recall.q: What did Sri Lanka's 2018 amendment change?
recall.a: It raised the age in section 75 of the Penal Code from eight to twelve.

recall.q: What does Pakistan's 2018 Act bar for juvenile offenders?
recall.a: Death sentences, fetters, handcuffs and corporal punishment.

recall.q: Who chairs Nepal's National Child Rights Council?
recall.a: The minister responsible for children (s. 59).

sections.title: Putting it to work
sections.big_idea: Twelve questions, one decision table and one worked case turn the law into **routes a field office can follow**.
in_plain_words: The design checklist asks who defines the child, who is excluded, how best interests are assessed, whether children were consulted, and whether a POCSO procedure and code of conduct exist. It continues with identification risk, district contacts, consent, children's data, a feedback route and follow-up.

The decision table pairs each situation with a law, a body and a time limit. Work the Raju and Salma case with it. **Start with a conversation with the child**, then follow a named staff member's follow-up, and avoid the seven common errors, from rescue without rehabilitation to consulting only once.

diagram.caption: the order of action in the worked case

key_terms.meaning: A written weighing of the child's interests in a decision about an individual child.
The child's own agreement alongside a parent's consent.
Child Marriage Prohibition Officer.
District Child Protection Unit.
A person with authority to act on child protection concerns.

worked_example.title: Choosing the route for Raju and Salma
worked_example.setup: Illustrative case: Raju, 13, washes dishes at an eatery from 6 pm to midnight. Salma, 16, has a wedding fixed for next month.
steps: Raju is under 14 and employed, so the labour ban applies and he is a child in need of care (JJ Act s. 2(14)(ii)).
Route for Raju: inform the labour inspector or police and the Child Welfare Committee, and plan income support first.
Salma is at imminent risk of marriage (JJ Act s. 2(14)(xii)), so any person can seek an injunction under PCMA s. 13.
For both, talk to the child first and name one staff member who owns the follow-up.
worked_example.answer: Raju goes to the labour inspector and Committee, Salma to the Prohibition Officer and magistrate, each after a conversation with the child.

mistakes: Quoting the CRC as if it were an Indian statute. Cite the Indian Act and use the CRC as an aid.
Rescue without rehabilitation, which returns children to work.
Treating every adolescent relationship as abuse and reporting without supporting both young people.
Consulting children once, at the end, which is tokenism.

recall.q: How many questions does the design checklist have?
recall.a: Twelve.

recall.q: How quickly must a child found working or begging be produced before a Committee?
recall.a: Within twenty-four hours, excluding travel time.

recall.q: Under which section can a girl at imminent risk of marriage be treated as a child in need of care?
recall.a: JJ Act section 2(14)(xii).

recall.q: When do the DPDP section 9 obligations apply?
recall.a: From 13 May 2027.

recall.q: Which General comment sets five budgeting principles?
recall.a: No. 19 (2016): effectiveness, efficiency, equity, transparency and sustainability.

sections.title: Participation, research and data
sections.big_idea: Hearing children is half of Article 12, and **research with children needs consent, assent and careful data**.
in_plain_words: Hart's ladder grades how far adults share decisions, from manipulation to projects children start. Lundy's four elements, Space, Voice, Audience and Influence, make a checklist. Participation can harm through tokenism, exposure, burden, exclusion and broken promises, and it faces the same best-interests test as anything else.

Under the ICMR 2017 guidelines, parents decide on participation, and assent is oral for ages 7 to 12 and written for 12 to 18. The DPDP Act requires verifiable parental consent from 13 May 2027. **Minimise, separate, protect, disclose and return**, and disaggregate by sex, age, caste, disability, residence and wealth.

diagram.caption: assent by age under the ICMR guidelines

key_terms.meaning: Eight rungs of participation from manipulation to child-initiated projects.
Space, Voice, Audience and Influence.
A child's own agreement to take part.
Legally acceptable representative.
Parental consent the data fiduciary can demonstrate, required by DPDP s. 9(1).
Splitting data by group so exclusion shows.

worked_example.title: What assent does each child need?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a survey includes children aged 5, 9 and 15.
steps: Age 5 is under 7, so no assent need be documented, though parents or the LAR decide on participation.
Age 9 is within 7 to 12, so verbal assent in the presence of parents or LAR is recorded.
Age 15 is within 12 to 18, so written assent is needed, also signed by parents or LAR.
In all three cases a child who objects must be respected, and failure to object is not assent.
worked_example.answer: No documented assent at 5, oral at 9, written at 15.

mistakes: Calling a child speaker at a conference participation when staff wrote the words.
Treating silence as assent. The guidelines say mere failure to object is not assent.
Promising confidentiality to participants. POCSO section 19 binds researchers who hear a disclosure.
Consulting only articulate, schooled, urban children.

recall.q: What are Lundy's four elements?
recall.a: Space, Voice, Audience and Influence.

recall.q: What does the ICMR require for a child aged 12 to 18?
recall.a: Written assent, also signed by the parents or LAR.

recall.q: What does DPDP section 9(3) bar?
recall.a: Tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children.

recall.q: What is the maximum penalty for breaching the section 9 obligations?
recall.a: Up to Rs 200 crore.

recall.q: Why must a consent script mention POCSO section 19?
recall.a: Because a researcher who hears a disclosure of sexual abuse is bound to report it.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a route map. The twelve sections move from why rights matter, through the treaty and Indian law, to practice and data. If you already work with children, start at section 11 for the checklist and return to the law sections as each question comes up.
notes.4: Treat the two frames as a test you can run on any document. Ask whether a child who is not helped has a complaint or only bad luck. **A rights frame names someone with a duty.** Most South Asian child policy mixes both, so read which one a scheme or log-frame actually uses.
notes.5: Use these four questions as a habit before design. Who is left out, whose interest decides, is the child safe, was the child heard. Each one maps to a Convention article. **Ask them before the design is fixed**, because a needs assessment alone tends to skip all four.
notes.6: Look at the kind of right each number measures. Stunting is a survival and development matter, and the crime count is a protection matter. **Registered crimes measure what reached the police.** A rise can mean more abuse, more reporting, or both, so never read it as a plain trend.
notes.7: Remember the families as survive, develop, be protected and take part, with non-discrimination and best interests running across all of them. The slide calls this a **teaching device**. Rights are indivisible in the Convention, so a child out of school is more exposed to labour and early marriage.
notes.8: Fill in the middle column for your own organisation. The last line carries the weight: once an NGO runs a home, a school or a helpline, it **carries statutory duties of its own**. POCSO section 19(1) reaches "any person", so the duty to report sexual offences belongs to everyone.
notes.9: This slide warns you about your own good intentions. Confining girls, raiding workplaces without follow-up and prosecuting two sixteen-year-olds are all done in a child's name. Apply the closing test: **would the child, once old enough to judge, agree it was done for them?**
notes.11: Fix three facts about the treaty: 54 articles, adoption on 20 November 1989 and 196 States parties. Part I holds the rights and Part II the monitoring. The US signed and has not ratified, and a signature carries only a duty to avoid defeating the treaty's purpose.
notes.12: Scan the Note column first. Every South Asian state is a party, but India alone **acceded without signing**, which has the same legal effect as ratification. Bangladesh and the Maldives entered reservations, so check the UN Treaty Collection for the current text before you quote any state's position.
notes.13: India accepted Article 32 on child labour with a promise to phase in minimum ages and left the timetable open. Read the declaration as a promise that civil society can press on. The slide links it forward to the 2016 child labour amendment as **the follow-through**.
notes.14: Notice two phrases: "within their jurisdiction" and the parent's status. Together they cover refugee, stateless and migrant children and stop a child being penalised for a father's caste. "Social origin" and "birth or other status" are the grounds that reach caste. **Equal treatment can still leave some children out.**
notes.15: Best interests is "a primary consideration", so weigh it heavily while other interests may also count. It reaches budgets, laws and private welfare institutions, which brings your NGO inside the rule. General comment 14 adds a **procedural test**: show how the child's interests were assessed.
notes.16: Article 6 has two halves. Paragraph 1 forbids taking a child's life, and paragraph 2 sets a duty to ensure survival and development "to the maximum extent possible". The stunting figures compare India at 29.3%, Nepal at 24.8% and Bangladesh at 23.6%. **Birth registration under Article 7 makes a child visible** to every scheme.
notes.17: Article 12 carries two duties, and programmes often meet only the first. A child must be able to speak, and the views must receive **due weight** according to age and maturity. Article 12(2) extends this to proceedings such as custody, adoption and a Child Welfare Committee inquiry.
notes.18: Use the grid as a design check. Each row is a situation and each column is one principle. **A blank cell is a question nobody on the team has answered.** Add a row for your own programme and fill all four cells before you start.
notes.20: Remember which protocol does what: OPAC on armed conflict, OPSC on sale and sexual exploitation, OPIC on complaints. The first two have 173 and 178 parties, and OPIC has 54. Only OPIC lets children bring complaints to the Committee, so its party count tells you most about remedies.
notes.21: Read the last column. All eight states accepted the two substantive protocols, and only the Maldives accepted the complaints procedure. For an Indian child **there is no route to the UN Committee**, so remedies run through Indian courts, the NCPCR and state commissions.
notes.22: Declared recruitment ages differ because the protocol allows voluntary recruitment below eighteen with safeguards. India says sixteen with deployment only at eighteen, Bangladesh sixteen or seventeen, Nepal and Sri Lanka eighteen. The rule on direct participation in hostilities applies to **everyone under eighteen**.
notes.23: The Committee has 18 experts, a first report due two years after entry into force and periodic reports every five years. It issues no binding judgments under the Convention itself. Its strength is publicity: **concluding observations give you a dated benchmark** to hold a government to at the next review.
notes.24: Follow the six steps and find where you fit. Practitioners enter at step two with an alternative report, and programme data, case files and children's own accounts make it the most concrete evidence the Committee sees. **Simplified reporting changes the order**, with questions sent before the state's report.
notes.25: India's last full review ended in concluding observations on 13 June 2014. As of October 2026 the fifth and sixth cycle has no adopted list of issues. Against a five-year rhythm, **that gap is itself a finding** you can state in an alternative report.
notes.26: A general comment is the Committee's authoritative reading of the text, which courts and donors use to fill gaps. Keep the five numbers close: 14, 19, 20, 24 and 26. For an NGO the useful part of No. 14 is the procedural rule: **ask to see the evaluation of the decision's impact on the child**.
notes.28: Sort the five articles by tier. Articles 15(3), 21A and 24 sit in Part III as fundamental rights, and Articles 39(e), 39(f) and 45 sit in Part IV as directive principles. Article 51A(k) adds a **parental duty** to provide education between six and fourteen.
notes.29: The tier decides what you can demand in court. Part III rights are enforceable through Article 226 or Article 32, while Part IV principles are read alongside Article 21 to give content. The consequence on the slide: **a four-year-old has a weaker constitutional claim than a six-year-old**.
notes.30: Follow the timeline to see why Article 21A exists. A 1950 promise of schooling to fourteen within ten years missed its target by decades. The 2002 amendment inserted Article 21A, and **the right works as the RTE Act shapes it**, which took effect on 1 April 2010.
notes.31: Treat the Sivakasi order as a pattern: a constitutional prohibition tied to money and to schooling. Employers paid into a fund used only for the child, an adult in the family got a job or Rs 5,000, and families offered jobs had to send the child to school. The 2016 district fund **follows the same logic**.
notes.32: Courts build child rights by reading Article 21 together with the directive principles and the CRC. Remember the two examples: 2017 on sex with a married girl under eighteen, and 2024 on child marriage, which stressed prevention. **The 2017 holding now sits in the new penal code**, section 63 Exception 2.
notes.33: Check which definition your programme works under, because the table shows nine different tests. The slide's example is **a fifteen-year-old domestic worker**, who is a child under the JJ Act and POCSO, an adolescent under labour law and outside the RTE Act's guarantee.
notes.35: Learn the two doors by who decides. A child in conflict with law goes to the Juvenile Justice Board, and a child in need of care goes to the Child Welfare Committee. **Age is fixed at the date of the offence.** A child can move between doors, as a working child picked up in a raid does.
notes.36: The sixteen principles bind NGOs running homes and shelters as well as government. Adopt two as working rules: institutionalisation as a last resort, and non-stigmatising semantics, so case files and donor updates avoid "juvenile delinquent" and "rescued girls". **Words in reports are part of compliance.**
notes.37: A Board has a Principal Magistrate and two social workers, at least one a woman. Remember what it must do: treat bail as the rule, choose orders from advice up to a special home for three years, and never impose death or life without release. **Offences are graded petty, serious, heinous.**
notes.38: This was the most contested change of 2015. For a heinous offence by a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old the Board assesses capacity, and the case may go to the Children's Court. Even then **there is no death sentence and no life without release**. General comment 24 recommends treating everyone under eighteen as a child.
notes.39: A Committee has a Chairperson and four members and decides whether a child needs care, where the child lives meanwhile, and the longer-term outcome. Many people can bring a child, who must be produced within twenty-four hours. **Informal placement without a Committee order leaves the child outside the Act's safeguards.**
notes.40: Read the table from the top: restoration to family is the default and the institution is the short-term option. Section 3(xii) makes institutionalisation a last resort. Sponsorship fits when poverty is the reason for separation, so **money can keep a family together**. After care covers the transition at eighteen.
notes.41: The 2021 amendment moved final adoption orders from civil courts to the District Magistrate and widened "serious offences". PRS asked whether an administrator should create a permanent legal relationship. The practical point is the gap: **a right to a Committee is empty in a district where none sits regularly**.
notes.42: The Act also punishes adults. Section 74 on identifying a child binds NGOs as much as newspapers, with up to six months or a fine of up to two lakh rupees. Check every case study, photograph and donor report before it goes out. Sections 75, 76 and 79 cover cruelty, begging and bondage.
notes.44: POCSO protects every person under eighteen without reference to sex, so boys have the same protection as girls. The Act brought three things the penal code lacked: graded offences, child-friendly procedure and a **duty on everyone to report**. The 69,191 cases in 2024 were 36.9% of crimes against children.
notes.45: Read the table in pairs, a definition section and then its punishment section, such as sections 3 and 4. Each main offence has an aggravated form, and **an offence by institution staff or a person in a position of trust counts as aggravated**. The 2019 amendment added the death of the child and natural calamity.
notes.46: Section 19 puts the duty on any person, including a child, and section 21 punishes failure, with up to one year for the head of an institution. A child cannot be punished for failing to report. **Tell young people before they disclose what you must report**, because mandatory reporting overrides confidentiality.
notes.47: This slide lists the safeguards in the order of a case: a statement at a place the child chooses, a Special Court, a presumption against the accused for listed offences, evidence within thirty days and a trial in a year. **Targets slip unless someone watches them**, so track each timeline in the case file.
notes.48: The 2019 amendment raised minimum sentences and added death as a possible sentence for aggravated penetrative assault. Child rights groups warned this could deter reporting, because offenders are often known to the child. Daily work changes little, but **families may weigh the decision to go to the police differently**.
notes.49: POCSO treats any sexual act with a person under eighteen as an offence, so a relationship between a seventeen-year-old and a nineteen-year-old can lead to a charge. The Law Commission kept the age at eighteen and proposed sentencing discretion. As of October 2026 that is **still only a recommendation**.
notes.50: Use the term CSEAM, child sexual exploitation and abuse material, because "pornography" suggests consent and a commercial product. The 2024 Supreme Court judgment held that viewing and storing can fall within section 15. For your organisation the rule is simple: **never forward suspected material**, even to report it.
notes.51: Follow the flow after a disclosure and find its weak point. The slide places it between the report and the trial, when a child can wait months with no counselling, schooling support or legal aid. **That is where a support organisation is most useful.** Note Child Helpline 1098.
notes.53: Pick out the entitlements you can check on a school visit: a neighbourhood school, no capitation fee or screening, no physical punishment, and a School Management Committee with at least three-fourths parents or guardians. Each is a constitutional entitlement for a child aged six to fourteen. **Grievances go to the local authority** under section 32.
notes.54: Section 12(1)(c) reserves at least twenty-five per cent of Class I seats in unaided private schools for disadvantaged and weaker-section children. Its value depends on state notification, timely reimbursement and checking that children stay. **Help families apply, then stay in touch through the first year.**
notes.55: Section 16 changed in 2019. The 2009 text barred holding back or expelling a child before elementary education ended. The amendment allows examinations in classes five and eight, then a re-examination within two months, and states may allow holding back. **The two-month remedial window is the protection to watch.**
notes.56: Section 17 bans physical punishment and mental harassment outright, yet both remain common. The RTE remedy is disciplinary action against the teacher, and the JJ Act adds criminal routes in section 75 and, for institutions, section 82. Train teachers in alternatives and **set up a complaint route a child can use safely**.
notes.57: Read the table by age. Under 14 there is a ban with two exceptions, family enterprise outside school hours and artists. From 14 to 18 only hazardous work is barred. **Parents are punished only if they permit work for commercial purposes.** Penalties run from six months to two years or Rs 20,000 to Rs 50,000.
notes.58: Set the two arguments side by side. Critics say the family exception legalises the work that is hardest to inspect, and supporters say a total ban would criminalise poor parents. The slide gives a practical test whatever the legal category: **is the child attending school regularly and learning?**
notes.59: State the source and date whenever you quote these counts. India's 10.1 million comes from Census 2011, and the next Census has a reference date of 1 March 2027. Globally 138 million children are in child labour, and Asia and the Pacific fell from 49 million to 28 million.
notes.60: Rescue is the first of five steps. After removal come the Committee, age determination and prosecution, the district fund, and restoration with school admission. Measure your programme by whether the child is **in school and out of work a year later**, and name one person who owns the follow-up.
notes.61: The table lines up three age bands against education law and labour law. The weak point is fourteen, when the RTE guarantee ends in the same year that non-hazardous work becomes lawful. **Track that transition by name** for every child who finishes class eight.
notes.63: Hold three definitions: a child is a woman under 18 or a man under 21, a child marriage is one where either party is a child, and the marriage is voidable at the option of the party who was a child. **Offences carry up to two years and a fine up to one lakh rupees.**
notes.64: Use the timeline to answer whether the age has changed. It rose to 18 and 21 in 1978 and was carried into the 2006 Act, and the 2021 Bill to raise women's age to 21 lapsed in June 2024. **The minimum ages remain 18 and 21** as of October 2026.
notes.65: Read the chart as one line per country and compare the direction of each line first. India's own headline figure is about 23 per cent in NFHS-5 and 20.1 per cent in NFHS-6. The measure is **women aged 20 to 24 looking back**, and survey years differ by country.
notes.66: The gradient carries the message. Women with no schooling marry before eighteen at 45.9% and those with secondary schooling at 26.9%, rural women at 25.8% and urban at 14.2%, West Bengal 41.5% against Kerala 6.3%. **These associations show where to look first**, though they show no cause.
notes.67: Think of the table as a toolkit for before the wedding. Anyone, or an NGO with reasonable information, can ask a Judicial Magistrate for an injunction, and courts can act without notice in urgency. **Find out who your district's prohibition officer is before you need one.**
notes.68: The 2024 judgment moves weight to prevention: awareness, school retention, support for girls who refuse, and working prohibition officers. It also invited Parliament to consider outlawing betrothals. The slide adds a caution: **prosecution can harm the girl the law protects**, so weigh best interests before pressing charges.
notes.69: Child marriage touches four other bodies of law. A wife under eighteen is protected by rape law since 2017, and POCSO applies regardless of marriage. A girl at imminent risk of marriage can be placed in safety by a Committee. **A birth certificate is the best evidence of age.**
notes.71: The NCPCR has a Chairperson and six members, and every state may set up its own commission. Commissions inquire into violations, may take suo motu notice and hold civil court powers during an inquiry. **The Act defines child rights to include the CRC's rights**, so it speaks the Convention's language.
notes.72: The same commissions monitor RTE section 31 and POCSO section 44, and the Commissions Act lets states designate Children's Courts for speedy trial. A complaint costs nothing and needs no lawyer. **Commissions recommend and do not enforce**, so track each recommendation and go to the High Court under Article 226 if nothing happens.
notes.73: ICDS began on 2 October 1975 and now runs as Anganwadi Services under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0. Learn the six services, three of which are health services delivered through NHM. Because Article 45 is a directive principle, **a child under six has no fundamental right to an anganwadi place**.
notes.74: Mission Vatsalya subsumed the Child Protection Services scheme and funds the bodies the JJ Act needs in each district. The Centre and State share costs 60:40 for most states, 90:10 for the North-East and some hill states and 100:0 for UTs without a legislature. **Use the current name and the guidelines of 5 July 2022.**
notes.75: The share of the Union Budget going to children has fallen by about half since 2012-13, although absolute allocations rose. The 2026-27 allocation is Rs 1,32,296.85 crore. Education takes 74 to 77 per cent and **protection only 1.49 to 1.73 per cent**.
notes.76: This is your one-page referral map. Match the need to the route: danger now means Child Helpline 1098 or police, a sexual offence means the police or Special Juvenile Police Unit, and a child out of school means the local authority, then the state commission. **A route with no named contact in the district will fail** on the day it is needed.
notes.78: Use the comparison table to see how definitions differ. India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Pakistan define a child as under 18 in their main laws, while Sri Lanka's Ordinance of 1939 defines a child as under 14 and a young person as under 16. **Each country also names different bodies.**
notes.79: Bangladesh's Children Act 2013 follows the Convention's pattern: a child is anyone up to eighteen, Child Welfare Boards sit at three levels and police stations have Child Affairs Desks. The gap the commentary names is that **cases against children still go to a judicial Children's Court**, with no independent non-judicial forum.
notes.80: Nepal's Act of 2018 sets out rights in the CRC's pattern and goes further in two places: protection from violence at home by family and teachers, and an express mention of untouchability-based mistreatment. Criminal responsibility starts at ten. **The caste wording gives practitioners a direct statutory hook.**
notes.81: Two reforms share this slide. Pakistan's 2018 Act bars death sentences, fetters and corporal punishment for juvenile offenders and creates diversion committees. Sri Lanka raised criminal responsibility from eight to twelve in 2018, yet the 1939 Ordinance leaves a gap for **sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds**.
notes.82: Compare the floors: India seven, Nepal ten and Sri Lanka twelve, while General comment 24 encourages at least fourteen. In India a child under eighteen is still dealt with under the JJ Act, so **the floor matters less in practice than the procedure**.
notes.84: Use the twelve questions to review one real programme. Each no points to a specific fix in the right-hand column. The first six cover the definition of a child, exclusion, best interests, consultation, a POCSO procedure and a code of conduct. **The last six cover communications, contacts, consent, data, feedback and follow-up.**
notes.85: Work this case before you read the routes. Raju is under fourteen and employed at night, and Salma is at imminent risk of marriage. The legal route differs for each, but the first step is the same: **talk to the child, then name a staff member who owns the follow-up**.
notes.86: Treat this as a lookup table for the field office. Note the time limits: 24 hours for police to inform the Committee and Special Court, 24 hours to produce a child before the Committee, and bail as the default. Practice is slower, so **someone must follow up** on every deadline.
notes.87: A rights programme can itself harm children, which is why POCSO treats an offence by staff as aggravated. The checklist includes a signed policy, safe recruitment, a safeguarding lead and a reporting route that bypasses the line manager. **A partner's lapse is reported under your organisation's name.**
notes.88: The six steps show when to act. Because the fifth and sixth cycle uses simplified reporting, input before the list of issues is adopted is most useful. Join a coalition, organise by article, and collect children's views with consent, assent and anonymity.
notes.89: Run the four-step budget exercise on one scheme: find it, compare estimate, revised estimate and actual spending for three years, divide by eligible children, then check what reached the district. Child protection is a small slice, and **underspending often means the posts and bodies are missing**.
notes.90: Read the right-hand column as habits to adopt. Seven errors recur: citing the CRC as Indian law, using an old scheme name, treating every adolescent relationship as abuse, rescue without rehabilitation, identifiable stories, consulting once and collecting too much data. **One named person asking the questions early prevents most of them.**
notes.92: Hart's ladder grades how far adults let children take part, from manipulation up to projects children start. Lundy's four words, Space, Voice, Audience and Influence, make a checklist for the end of any consultation. Remember her point: **hearing children is only half of Article 12**.
notes.93: The Bhima Sangha example shows children organising themselves. Reddy and Ratna added two rungs below Hart's lowest, active resistance and hindrance, and named tolerance and indulgence as tokenism. Nepal's law gives children a right to join decisions and form clubs, so **plan protection for members who speak against adults**.
notes.94: Use the risk table as a pre-mortem for any consultation. The five risks are tokenism, exposure, burden, exclusion and broken promises. The test comes from Article 3: **a consultation that leaves a child less safe has failed**, however good the report looks. Report back, including when the answer is no.
notes.95: Memorise the assent bands: under 7 no assent need be documented, 7 to 12 oral and recorded, 12 to 18 written and also signed by a parent. Parents or the legal representative decide on participation. **Failure to object is never assent**, and a child's objection must be respected.
notes.96: Four practical points: the ethics committee decides whether one or both parents must consent, institutions give their own permission, assent forms use simple language, and children in homes under the JJ Act need the Committee's role considered. **Tell participants before the interview what you will have to report.**
notes.97: DPDP section 9 requires verifiable parental consent, bars tracking and targeted advertising aimed at children, and carries a penalty up to Rs 200 crore. The date matters: **these obligations apply from 13 May 2027** and are not in force as of October 2026. The research exemption may not cover surveys that target named children.
notes.98: Five habits for child data are minimise, separate, protect, disclose and return. Add a sixth, disaggregate, because Article 2 cannot be monitored without data by sex, age, caste, disability, residence and wealth. **Ask whose voice a dataset carries**: early marriage figures come from women looking back.
notes.99: Pick your next course by your gap. Safeguarding & PSEA suits a field visit coming up, Research Ethics suits consent design, and Data Protection & the DPDP Act suits personal data. The slide offers a **two-step plan**: run the Section 11 checklist on a programme you know, then read the safeguarding deck.
